description_full: Pursuit Attractions and Hospitality, Inc., an attraction and hospitality company, owns and operates a collection of travel experiences in iconic destinations in the United States, Canada, Iceland, and Costa Rica. It operates various attractions and lodges with integrated restaurants, retail, and transportation facilities, as well as owns and operates eco-luxury resorts. The company was formerly known as Viad Corp and changed its name to Pursuit Attractions and Hospitality, Inc. in January 2025. Pursuit Attractions and Hospitality, Inc. was founded in 1926 and is based in Denver, Colorado.
ceo_bio: Mr. David W. Barry | President, CEO & Director | Age 62 | Compensation: $1.6M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 2K people. Revenue per employee of $215K ranks in the bottom quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, with revenue falling 5%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $5K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 8× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Pursuit Attractions and Hospita is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $1.5B market cap on $452M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -26% over the past three years and -8% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $11M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.80× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 7.2×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.7%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 60% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 8% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $9.24 (margin of safety -486%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 6%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $7.95 to $18.56 (P10-P90).

Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 47% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $64.86 on average, 20% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.8%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 3.42).

The current ratio of 0.81 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
It runs on negative working capital (-86 days), so customers and suppliers effectively fund its operations.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -26.2% over 3 years, 1.7% over 5 years and -8.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 43%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex runs 1.6x depreciation (16.6% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 3, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect -1.7% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.0%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).

Shareholder yield is a modest 0.7% (0.7% in buybacks).
